subtopic: Atomic Number and Atomic Mass Number
stem: Find out the number of protons, electrons and neutrons in the nuclide \(^{40}_{18}\mathrm{Ar}\).
solution:
In case of the nuclide \(^{40}_{18}\mathrm{Ar}\),

\(A = 40\) and \(Z = 18\)

Number of protons = number of electrons = \(Z = 18\) and number of neutrons

\(N = A - Z = 40 - 18 = 22\)

stem: The two natural isotopes of chlorine, viz. \(^{35}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}\) and \(^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}\) exist in relative abundance of 3:1. Find out the average atomic mass of chlorine.
solution:
From the relative abundance 3:1, it is understood that out of 4 chlorine atoms, 3 atoms have mass 35 and 1 has mass 37.

Therefore, the average atomic mass of chlorine

\(= \dfrac{3 \times 35 + 1 \times 37}{4} = 35.5\)

stem: Three elements Q, R and T have mass number 40. Their atoms contain 22, 21 and 20 neutrons, respectively. Represent their atomic composition with appropriate symbol.

subtopic: Developments Leading to the Bohr Model
stem:
Visible light has wavelengths ranging from 400 nm (violet) to 750 nm (red). Express these wavelengths in terms of frequency (Hz).

(1 nm \(= 10^{-9}\) m)
solution:
\(c = \nu\lambda\)  \(\therefore \nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda}\)

\(\therefore\) frequency of violet light \(= \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}}{400 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}} = 7.50 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}\)

and frequency of red light \(= \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}}{750 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}} = 4.00 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}\)

subtopic: Developments Leading to the Bohr Model
stem: Parameters of blue and red light are 400 nm and 750 nm respectively. Which of the two is of higher energy ?
solution:
400 nm and 750 nm are the wave lengths of blue and red light, respectively. Energy of radiation is given by the expression \(E = h\nu\) and \(\nu\), the frequency, of radiation is related to the wavelength by the expression.

\(\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda}\)

Therefore, shorter the wavelength, \(\lambda\), larger the frequency, \(\nu\), and higher the energy, \(E\). Thus, blue light which has shorter \(\lambda\) (400 nm) than red light (750 nm) has higher energy.

subtopic: Bohr's Model for the Hydrogen Atom
stem: How many electrons are present in \(^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H}\), \(_{2}\mathrm{He}\) and \(\mathrm{He^{\oplus}}\) ? Which of these are hydrogen like specis?
solution:
Hydrogen-like species contain only one electron.

\(^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H}\) number of protons = 1 = number of electrons

\(_{2}\mathrm{He}\) : number of protons = 2 = number of electrons

\(\mathrm{He^{\oplus}}\) : (number of electron in He) \(-\) 1 = (number of electron in \(\mathrm{He^{\oplus}}\)) = (2 - 1) = 1

Thus \(^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H}\) and \(\mathrm{He^{\oplus}}\) are hydrogen-like species.
_note: p-07 left column, printed p.42. The stem's 'specis' is the book's own spelling and is transcribed as printed.

subtopic: Bohr's Model for the Hydrogen Atom
stem: Calculate the radius and energy associated with the first orbit of \(\mathrm{He^{\oplus}}\).
solution:
[Textbook note (not an error): the question asks for BOTH the radius and the energy of the first orbit of \(\mathrm{He^{\oplus}}\), but the book's printed working stops the radius line at the unevaluated fraction \(\dfrac{52.9 \times 1^2}{2}\) and never states a value, so as printed only half the question is answered. The expression is correct and evaluating it gives \(r_1 = 26.45\ \mathrm{pm}\), which is the missing answer. The printed line is preserved exactly as it appears. The energy part is complete and correct: \(-2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times \dfrac{2^2}{1^2} = -8.72 \times 10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}\).]

\(\mathrm{He^{\oplus}}\) is a hydrogen-like species having the nuclear charge \(Z = 2\) and for the first orbit \(n = 1\)

radius of first orbit of \(\mathrm{He^{\oplus}}\)

\(r_1 = \dfrac{52.9(n^2)}{Z} = \dfrac{52.9 \times 1^2}{2}\)

Energy of first orbit of \(\mathrm{He^{\oplus}}\)

\(E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\left(\dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}\right)\ \mathrm{J}\)

\(= -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\left(\dfrac{2^2}{1^2}\right)\)

\(= -8.72 \times 10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}\)
_note: p-07 right column, printed p.42. The book stops the radius line at the unevaluated fraction and never states 26.45 pm; preserved as printed and completed in an errata bracket.

subtopic: Bohr's Model for the Hydrogen Atom
stem: What is the wavelength of the photon emitted during the transition from the orbit of \(n = 5\) to that of \(n = 2\) in hydrogen atom?
solution:
The wavenumber of transition is given by Rydberg expression

\(\bar{\nu} = 109677\left[\dfrac{1}{n_1^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^{2}}\right]\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)

Here \(n_1 = 2\) and \(n_2 = 5\)

\(\therefore\ \bar{\nu} = 109677\left[\dfrac{1}{2^2} - \dfrac{1}{5^2}\right]\)

\(= 109677\left[\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{25}\right]\)

\(= 109677 \times \dfrac{21}{100} = 23032.17\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{1}{23032.17}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\bar{\nu}} = 4.34 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm}\)

wavelength of photon

\(\lambda = 4.34 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm} = 4.34 \times 10^{-5} \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{nm} = 434\ \mathrm{nm}\)

subtopic: Quantum Mechanical Model of the Atom
stem: How many orbitals make the N shell? What is the subshell wise distribution of orbitals in the N shell?
solution:
For N shell principal quantum number \(n = 4\) \(\therefore\) Total number of orbitals in N shell \(= n^2 = 4^2 = 16\). The total number of subshells in N shell \(= n = 4\). The four subshells with their azimuthal quantum numbers and the constituent orbital number are as shown below

| Azimuthal quantum number \(l\) | Symbol of subshell | number of orbitals \(2l + 1\) |
|---|---|---|
| \(l = 0\) | s | \((2 \times 0) + 1 = 1\) |
| \(l = 1\) | p | \((2 \times 1) + 1 = 3\) |
| \(l = 2\) | d | \((2 \times 2) + 1 = 5\) |
| \(l = 3\) | f | \((2 \times 3) + 1 = 7\) |

subtopic: Quantum Mechanical Model of the Atom
stem: An atom has two electrons in its 4s orbital. Write the values of the four quantum numbers for each of them.
solution:
For the 4s orbital 4 stands for the principal quantum number \(n\); s stands for the subshell s having the value of azimuthal quantum number \(l = 0\). In the 's' subshell there is only one orbital and has magnetic quantum number \(m_l = 0\). The two electrons in this orbital have opposite spins. Thus the four quantum numbers of two electrons in 4s orbital are :

| | \(n\) | \(l\) | \(m_l\) | \(m_s\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| electron 1 | 4 | 0 | 0 | \(+1/2\) |
| electron 2 | 4 | 0 | 0 | \(-1/2\) |

subtopic: Quantum Mechanical Model of the Atom
stem: Write electronic configuration of \(_{18}\mathrm{Ar}\) and \(_{19}\mathrm{K}\) using orbital notation and orbital diagram method.
solution:
From the atomic numbers it is unterstood that 18 electron are to be filled in Ar atom and 19 electrons are to be filled in K atom. These are to be filled in the orbitals according to the aufbau principle. The electronic configuration of these atoms can be represented as.

| | Orbital notation | Orbital diagram |
|---|---|---|
| \(_{18}\mathrm{Ar}\) | \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\ 3s^2 3p^6\) | 1s \(\uparrow\downarrow\) ; 2s \(\uparrow\downarrow\) ; 2p \(\uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\) ; 3s \(\uparrow\downarrow\) ; 3p \(\uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\) |
| \(_{19}\mathrm{K}\) | \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\ 3s^2 3p^6 4s^1\) | 1s \(\uparrow\downarrow\) ; 2s \(\uparrow\downarrow\) ; 2p \(\uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\) ; 3s \(\uparrow\downarrow\) ; 3p \(\uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\) ; 4s \(\uparrow\) |
_note: p-18 top, printed p.53. The book draws the orbital diagram as boxed arrows; rendered here as a linear per-subshell arrow list, which carries the same information. 'unterstood' is the book's own spelling.

subtopic: Quantum Mechanical Model of the Atom
stem: Find out one dinegative anion and one unipositive cation which are isoelectronic with Ne atom. Write their electronic configuration using orbital notations and orbital digram method.
solution:
Ne has \(Z = 10\). Therefore Ne and its isoelectronic species contain 10 electrons each. The dinegative anionic species isoelectronic with Ne is obtained by adding two electrons to the atom with \(Z = 8\). This is \(\mathrm{O^{2\ominus}}\). The unipositive cationic species isoelectronic with Ne is obtained by removing one electron from an atom of \(Z = 11\). It is \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\). These species and their electronic configuration are shown below :

| | Number of electron | Orbital Notation | Orbital diagram |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ne | 10 | \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\) | 1s \(\uparrow\downarrow\) ; 2s \(\uparrow\downarrow\) ; 2p \(\uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\) |
| \(\mathrm{O} + 2e^{\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{O^{2\ominus}}\) | 10 | \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\) | 1s \(\uparrow\downarrow\) ; 2s \(\uparrow\downarrow\) ; 2p \(\uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\) |
| \(\mathrm{Na} - e^{\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) | 10 | \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\) | 1s \(\uparrow\downarrow\) ; 2s \(\uparrow\downarrow\) ; 2p \(\uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\ \uparrow\downarrow\) |

The book prints the three species in one table with a single shared 'Orbital Notation' cell and a single shared orbital diagram; that shared cell is repeated on each row here.
_note: p-18, printed p.53. 'digram' is the book's own spelling in the stem.
